content.prompt: Sketch the graph of $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ on the same axes, then graph $f(x)+g(x)$.

spec.description: Unnumbered axes; blue y=x; red y=|x| with a dashed negative-x ray. The positive rays coincide. Green supplied answer omitted.
spec.mathematics: f(x)=x and g(x)=|x| on unrestricted domains. No grid or numeric ticks.

answer.worked:
Both base graphs have their $x$- and $y$-intercepts at $(0,0)$. They coincide at every point $(t,t)$ with $t\geq0$.

For $x<0$, the ordinates are opposites, so their sum is zero. For $x>0$, the ordinates are equal, so their sum is twice either ordinate. For example, at $x=-1$ the sum is $-1+1=0$; at $x=1$ it is $1+1=2$.

Draw a horizontal ray along the negative $x$-axis and the ray $y=2x$ for $x\geq0$, meeting at $(0,0)$.

answer.worked:
Both base graphs have their $x$- and $y$-intercepts at $(0,0)$ and intersect at $(-1,-1)$, $(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$.

Add their ordinates at each common $x$-coordinate. At $x=-1$, the sum is $-1+(-1)=-2$; at $x=0$, it is $0$; at $x=1$, it is $1+1=2$.

Plot $(-1,-2)$, $(0,0)$ and $(1,2)$, then continue adding ordinates to sketch the increasing curve. Both ordinates are negative for $x<0$ and positive for $x>0$, so the sum crosses both axes only at $(0,0)$.
